title: What Humidity Level Does Mold Grow At?
h1: What Humidity Level Does Mold Grow At?
description: Mold tends to grow when indoor humidity stays high, especially on cool surfaces. Learn the humidity range to aim for and how to keep your home in it all year.
quick_answer: Mold can start growing when relative humidity stays above about 60 percent for long stretches, and the risk rises the higher it goes and the longer it stays there. Cool surfaces where condensation forms are the most vulnerable. Keeping indoor humidity roughly between 30 and 50 percent, as the EPA recommends, makes mold much less likely.
body:
Mold spores are everywhere, indoors and out. They only become a problem when they land somewhere with enough moisture to grow. Humidity is one of the biggest factors, but it's not the only one. The temperature of surfaces, airflow and how long things stay damp all matter.

What humidity range should you aim for?

The EPA recommends keeping indoor relative humidity below 60 percent, ideally between 30 and 50 percent. Within that range, most homes stay comfortable and mold, dust mites and condensation are less of a concern.

Below that range, the air gets dry enough to irritate skin, eyes and sinuses. Above it, especially when humidity stays high for days at a time, mold and dust mites have a much easier time.

To see where your home stands, use a hygrometer. A digital one is inexpensive and easy to use. Put one in a main living area and another in a room you're concerned about, like a bathroom or a bedroom with a musty smell. Check them at different times of day and in different seasons. Many smart thermostats also show indoor humidity.

Why do some spots grow mold even when the room seems fine?

Relative humidity changes with temperature. A room might read 55 percent in the middle, but the air touching a cold window, an exterior wall corner or the back of a closet is cooler, so the humidity right at that surface is higher. If it reaches the dew point, water condenses on the surface. That's why mold often shows up:

  • Around window frames and sliding doors.
  • In closets on exterior walls.
  • Behind furniture pushed against outside walls.
  • On bathroom ceilings and around showers.
  • Around AC supply registers where cold air meets humid room air.
  • Under sinks and around water heaters.

What raises humidity in Southern California homes?

Our climate varies a lot from the coast to inland valleys. Common sources include:

  • Coastal air. Homes near the ocean deal with marine layer moisture, especially in late spring and early summer.
  • Everyday living. Showers, cooking, laundry, plants and aquariums all add moisture.
  • Poor ventilation. Bathroom fans that don't vent outside, or that never get turned on.
  • Dryer vent problems. A disconnected vent can dump moist air into the house, garage or attic.
  • Leaks. Slow plumbing leaks and roof leaks add moisture where you can't see it.
  • An oversized AC. A system that short cycles cools the air without running long enough to pull out much moisture.

How do you bring humidity down?

  1. Use exhaust fans. Run bathroom fans during and after showers, and use the kitchen hood when cooking.
  2. Fix leaks quickly. Even small drips add up.
  3. Check the dryer vent. Make sure it's connected and venting outside.
  4. Let your AC do its part. A properly sized, well-maintained system removes moisture as it cools. Variable-speed systems that run longer at lower speeds are especially good at it.
  5. Add a dehumidifier. Portable units work for a room. A whole-home dehumidifier connected to your HVAC system handles the entire house.
  6. Improve air movement. Leave a little space between furniture and exterior walls, and keep closet doors open now and then.

Can a home be too dry?

Yes, and inland homes see it more often, especially during Santa Ana winds when outdoor humidity can drop very low. Dry air can leave you with itchy skin, static shocks, scratchy throats and cracked wood furniture or floors. If your hygrometer reads well below 30 percent for days at a time, a humidifier can help. The goal is the middle range, not as dry as possible.

What if you already see mold?

Small spots on hard surfaces like tile can often be cleaned with soap and water. If mold covers a large area, keeps coming back, or there's a musty smell you can't trace, look for the moisture source. If it's in your HVAC system, such as on the coil, in the drain pan or in the ducts, that needs professional attention. faqs: Can mold grow at 50 percent humidity?
It is much less likely in the room air at 50 percent. Mold can still grow on cold surfaces where condensation forms, or where a leak keeps materials wet, even if the room reading looks normal.
What humidity should I keep my house at?
Aim for about 30 to 50 percent relative humidity, and keep it below 60 percent. That range is comfortable for most people and discourages mold and dust mites.
Does running the AC reduce humidity?
Yes. Your AC removes moisture as it cools. An oversized or short-cycling system removes less, and a whole-home dehumidifier can help homes that stay damp.
Where should I put a humidity monitor?
Start in a main living area, then add one to any room that smells musty or shows condensation, like a bathroom or bedroom on an exterior wall.
